Market for salespeople the same way you market for customers. Your job ad is an ad. Your

TOOL 01 · PAY

embedded_text:
TOOL 01 · PAY

WHAT ALEX SAID ABOUT COMP
Five rules. The first two decide the shape of the plan. The third and fourth decide the number. The
fifth is the one change Alex says reliably improved his teams.
R ULE 1. KNOW WHICH KIND OF TEAM YOU HAVE

If your reps generate their own leads (door knocking, self-sourced outreach), that is a self-gen team.
Pay is pure commission. Whatever you pay that rep is your full cost to get a customer, which is why selfgen reps are paid the most. It is one of the hardest jobs.
If you hand your reps leads from anywhere else (ads, content, an outreach team, affiliates), that is a
lead-fed team. Pay is a 50/50 split between base salary and commission. Alex took this from Vista
Equity's analysis of its portfolio and says it has held up for him.
WHY 50/50

Pure commission on a lead-fed team is, in Alex's words, too commission-breathy. One bad month
and the rep cannot pay rent, so they leave. The base covers their basic needs. The commission
pays for their lifestyle.

R ULE 2. EVERY SALES ROLE HAS AN OTE

OTE is on-target earnings: what the rep makes in a year if they convert the leads they should convert.
You set the OTE first and build the plan backward from it.
R ULE 3. PROCESS SETS THE SKILL LEVEL. SKILL LEVEL SETS THE PAY

The more process you have (a strong brand, an education sequence, a great offer, a script), the less skill
the rep needs, and the less you have to pay. If you have no process, you need a rainmaker who can
drag a stranger from unaware to closed, and rainmakers cost several hundred thousand dollars a year.
Every dollar you save on rep skill is a dollar you can reinvest in growth.
R ULE 4. THE ONLY TEST OF A COMP PLAN

Can I attract the level of talent I need at this price? That is the whole question.
ALEX HORMOZI

Percentage of revenue, flat fee per deal, total deal volume: Alex says he does not care which method
you use. What matters is whether the number attracts the right person.
R ULE 5. TIE COMMISSION TO CASH COLLECTED UP FRONT

This is the one comp change Alex says has reliably increased close quality and pulled cash forward. Pay
on cash collected, not on contract value.

THE NUMBERS AND THE TRAP
Alex called these the ugliest estimate he could give. They depend on your market, ticket size, how
much process you have, and how replaceable the rep is. Use them as anchors, then adjust with Rule
3.

Depends on ticket size and how
replaceable they are.

W HY THE RANGE IS SO WIDE

A real estate agent earning 6% on a $20 million building and a car wash attendant upselling a dollar to
200 cars a day are both salespeople. Skill required, ticket size, number of at-bats, and how much
process sits behind the rep all move the number. If the rep says the same six lines all day, that is not a lot
of skill. If they have to get six decision makers to sign a three-year enterprise contract, it is.
T HE TRAP

Picking a percentage first. The playbook example of how this goes wrong: someone says "let's just make
it 10%," a rep has a huge week, and the owner realizes the plan pays out far more than the business can
carry. Cutting comp after the fact is the most expensive mistake on this list. The worksheet on the next
pages exists so you never pick the number first.

REMEMBER

Comp is not a formula. It is an offer to a specific caliber of person. Decide the caliber, then the number,
then the mechanics.

OTE $120,000. The rep should close 10 deals a month at $20,000 each, so $200,000 in cash a month.
The variable half of OTE is $60,000 a year, or $5,000 a month. $5,000 ÷ $200,000 = 2.5%. (The

STEP 7. BREAK IT, THEN SELL IT

Try to break it. If I were a rep on this plan, how would I game it? Anything paid on a number the rep

WHAT ALEX SAID ABOUT FINDING REPS
Whatever got you your first closer, do more of it. If you can't, it is one of three reasons: you don't know
your numbers, you think you can't afford it, or you don't have the bandwidth. This tool handles all
three.
T HE NUMBER YOU ARE MISSING: LTGP TO CAT

You know LTV to CAC for customers. Alex applies the same ratio to hires: lifetime gross profit per
employee against the cost of acquiring talent.

Don't be cheap with your growth. You're stealing from tomorrow for today.
ALEX HORMOZI

" I CAN'T AFFORD IT"

Run the exercise above with your own numbers. If a rep produces gross profit every year and you would
pay a fraction of that for any other asset with the same return, the recruiting budget is not a cost. It is the
cheapest asset you will buy this year.
" I DON'T HAVE THE BANDWIDTH"

Ask what it is costing you. Three reps at $250,000 a year each is $750,000. Is whatever you are doing
instead worth more than that? Sometimes the honest answer is that recruiting is not your constraint
right now. Alex's rule is to let fires burn until they become the constraint, then solve them. But if sales
capacity is the constraint, this is the project, and everything else waits.
Y OUR JOB AD IS AN AD

If you are not getting interest, the ad is weak. Alex's advice: take the structure of a job ad that is already
working and rewrite it for your culture. Do not copy it word for word, because your company is not his
company.

embedded_text:
TOOL 03 · INTERVIEW

WHAT ALEX SAID ABOUT SCREENING
F OR HIGH-VOLUME ROLES, ALWAYS BE INTERVIEWING

SDRs and setters turn over. That is the nature of the role. The mistake is running recruiting on and off: hire
three, stop, lose two, panic, start again. If the role is high-volume, interviewing is a standing process, not
a project.
S CREEN IN GROUPS, NOT ONE ON ONE

One-on-one calls for entry-level roles are not efficient. Alex means entry-level in skill, not in worth as a
person. Group screening lets you see ten people in the time a single call takes, and you see how they
perform in front of others.
T HE PROCESS ALEX RUNS
S TEP

W HAT HAPPENS

W HAT IT FILTERS FOR

1. Apply

Candidate applies through your ad.

Interest.

2. Send the script

If you like the application, send them a piece of your
sales script.

Follow-through.

3. Video back

They record themselves delivering it. About 60 seconds.
The intro, the opener, whatever you choose.

Can they deliver? Do they take
direction?

4. Group interview

Invite the good videos to one group session.

Presence in a room.

5. Role play

One to two minutes each, in front of the group.

Live skill under pressure.

6. Feedback

Give feedback on the spot.

How they take coaching.

7. Follow-up call

The ones who did well get a one-on-one.

Fit.

8. Offer

Make the offer with the comp plan from Tool 01.

IF YOU NEED A SUPERSTAR CLOSER

This is an SDR process. For a top closer you do the opposite: one-on-one outreach, one-on-one
call. But once they are in, everyone starts at the bottom and hits the same KPIs. Closers get
earmarked to move up faster. Nobody skips the line, because everyone needs to be able to hunt.

TOOL 04 · PROMOTE

WHAT ALEX SAID ABOUT KEEPING THEM
R EPEATED ROLES NEED MORE RUNGS

Sales, support, editing: any role you have many people in is repetitive. Alex says it took him a long time to
figure this out. The fix is multiple tiers of title with small comp changes at each one, so people get regular
reinforcement and something to look forward to. Three tiers of title (junior, the title itself, senior) with a
comp bump inside each gives you five increments of reward. Roughly every 12 weeks, someone can
earn a step.
A LEX'S LADDER
T RACK

J UNIOR

T ITLE

S ENIOR

M ANAGER

Junior SDR

SDR

Senior SDR

SDR Manager

Closer track

Junior Closer

Closer

Senior Closer

Closer Manager

From Closer Manager, people can branch into other paths in the company. And a Senior SDR moving to Junior Closer is a real
promotion for most people. Not everyone should aim for manager, because the numbers don't work: you cannot have as
many managers as reps.

S TEPS ARE EARNED BY CUMULATIVE REPS

The milestones are mostly about volume. Alex's example, with placeholder numbers:

25

50

100

200

D EALS

D EALS

D EALS

D EALS

Comp bump. Same title.

Junior SDR becomes SDR.

Comp bump. Same title.

SDR becomes Senior SDR.

Comp changes.

Better hours, better leads.

PERKS COST LESS THAN RAISES

Every step does not need to be money. For salespeople the perks Alex reaches for are better leads
and better hours. For editors it would be better content. Small, real, and tied to the title.

Q UALIFIED, NOT ENTITLED

Hitting the number means you are qualified for the promotion, not owed it. You still have to be a strong
contributor and a cultural fit. Alex is direct about this: nobody on the team should feel entitled to
anything. Everything is earned.

Think about what they go home and say. "I got a promotion." "I keep moving up." That is
what keeps someone in a repetitive job.
ALEX HORMOZI, PARAPHRASED
